title: The CBAM Policy Tool

slides.title: The CBAM Policy Tool
slides.subtitle: What the EU's carbon border charge will cost exporters, and which lever cuts it
slides.message: For dirty goods most of the EU's border charge arrives in 2026. Verified data, cleaner production and a domestic carbon price can each cut it, but the right lever differs by product: for Egypt, data cut the charge on steel by about 90 percent and on urea by 13 percent.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.text: Since January 2026 EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity owe certificates for embedded emissions; importers below 50 tonnes a year are exempt. A July 2026 proposal (not adopted) would end the phase-in in 2038, cutting the 2034 charge to €236.

slides.title: Exporting governments control three levers on the bill

points.text: Without them the EU applies a country default plus a mark-up of 10% in 2026 rising to 30% from 2028 (1% for fertilizers).
Every tonne of CO₂ cut per tonne of product saves the certificate price.
A price "effectively paid" is deducted one for one, and the money stays at home.

points.lead: But a rebated price earns nothing.
points.text: The draft rules net off rebates and emissions below a baseline, so a feebate gets no deduction.
